questions.question_text: Which statement correctly defines the relationship between the derivative $f'(a)$ and the graph of $y = f(x)$?

options.text: $f'(a)$ is the gradient of the tangent line to the curve at $x = a$.
$f'(a)$ is the $y$-value of the curve at $x = a$.
options.why: Confuses the derivative $f'(a)$ with the function value $f(a)$.

options.text: $f'(a)$ is the gradient of the secant line between $x = 0$ and $x = a$.
options.why: Confuses the instantaneous tangent gradient with a secant from the origin.

options.text: $f'(a)$ is the area under the curve between $x = 0$ and $x = a$.
options.why: Confuses differentiation with integration.

questions.solution_text: $\text{By definition, the derivative } f'(a)\text{ is the gradient of the tangent line to } y = f(x)\text{ at } x = a.$

questions.question_text: How can the approximation of the instantaneous rate of change at $x = 2$ using the average rate over $[2, 2+h]$ be improved?

options.text: By making the interval width $h$ smaller and closer to $0$.
By making the interval width $h$ larger.
options.why: Larger intervals deviate further from the local tangent slope.

options.text: By averaging the function values $f(2)$ and $f(2+h)$.
options.why: Averaging function values gives the average of the two endpoint heights, not a gradient.

options.text: By changing the base point from $x = 2$ to $x = 0$.
options.why: Changing the base point evaluates the rate at a different location.
